extracted.intended_audience: editors, authors, and peer reviewers of peer-reviewed biomedical/medical journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and implementing conflict-of-interest (COI) policies for peer-reviewed medical journals, covering definitions, types of competing interests, disclosure procedures, management, and enforcement. Intended to direct journal editors (and inform authors/reviewers) on best practices for transparency and handling COI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of conflict of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear definition the journal uses as to what is conflict of interest and who is captured in the definition. Sample definition: conflict of interest exists when a participant in the publication process (author, peer reviewer or editor) has a competing interest that could unduly influence (or be reasonably seen to do so) his or her responsibilities in the publication process (submission of manuscripts, peer review, editorial decisions, and communication between authors, reviewers and editors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should articulate who is covered (authors, reviewers, editors) and which publication-process activities are implicated (submission, review, editorial decisions, communications). Provide an explicit, easily understood definition so that participants can self-assess whether they are captured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit listing of types of competing interests (policy scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear statement of examples of the types of competing interests (and their definitions) the journal says must be declared. The statement should include examples such as financial ties, academic commitments, personal relationships, political or religious beliefs, and institutional affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give examples and definitions of what competing interests should be declared; recognize a wide range and that multiple interests can coexist. Move beyond a narrow focus on financial COI so declarers understand breadth of reportable interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial ties (including clinical income)
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial ties to industry/companies that sell healthcare products and other financial interests that could bias judgment. WAME explicitly expands financial conflict to include the effects of clinical income (e.g., physicians whose livelihood depends on specific procedures or diagnostics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that financial incentives are especially powerful and not always obvious; include diverse financial relationships and income sources (grants, consulting, royalties, stock ownership, clinical fees) when defining reportable interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic commitments / intellectual passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-financial conflict arising from scholarly commitment: 'intellectual passion,' the tendency to favor positions that one has already espoused or perhaps even established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat strong intellectual or scholarly commitments as potential competing interests to be declared; these can bias interpretation and should be recognized alongside financial interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts stemming from personal relationships: the tendency to judge the works of friends/colleagues or competitors/foes differently because of the relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require disclosure of personal relationships that could reasonably be seen to affect objectivity in reviewing or editorial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political or religious beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-financial conflicts related to political or religious beliefs: the tendency to favor or reject positions because they affirm or challenge one's political or religious convictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include ideological or belief-based interests in the policy so that contributors disclose whether such beliefs could reasonably appear to affect their responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts arising from institutional affiliations: the tendency to favor or reject results of research because of one's institutional ties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors, reviewers, and editors to disclose institutional roles, leadership positions, or institutional incentives that might be perceived as competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope across participants (authors, reviewers, editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict-of-interest policies should address all participants in the research and publication continuum, including authors, peer reviewers, and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure policies explicitly cover reviewers and editors (not only authors). Note: conflicts between editors and owners may require additional or separate policy statements (WAME addresses editorial independence separately).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for declaring conflicts (what, when, to whom, and format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear statements on: (I) what is to be declared, when and to whom; (II) format for declaration; (III) a journal’s role in asking additional questions or seeking clarification about disclosures; and, (IV) consequences for failing to disclose before or after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should design disclosure forms/questions to maximize relevant reporting, specify timing (submission, revision, post-publication), state the recipient (editor, publisher), and define the required format. Because routine monitoring is impractical, place onus on declarers and construct questions to elicit comprehensive reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active elicitation and clarification of disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should have a role in asking additional questions or seeking clarification about disclosures to ensure completeness and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because journals cannot routinely verify all facts, they should use targeted questions, follow up on ambiguous disclosures, and seek clarification when necessary to obtain uncensored information enabling editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of disclosed conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear statement on how conflict of interest will be managed by the journal, including the position that all relevant conflict of interest disclosures (or the declaration of no conflict of interest) will be published with the article and clarity about what conflict of interest situations will result in a manuscript not being considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the range of actions (e.g., disclosure only, exclusion from review, independent review, rejection) and specify which situations lead to exclusion. Make management rules known to all participants to avoid ad hoc decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing disclosures and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should publish with every article all relevant author disclosures (or a declaration of no conflict of interest) so readers have transparent information about competing interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency to readers is essential; include disclosures in articles or linked statements. Lack of published disclosures undermines reader trust and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility to investigate and act on nondisclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have a responsibility for investigating, and if relevant acting, if competing interests surface after a manuscript is submitted or published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat allegations of failure to disclose seriously; investigate promptly and take appropriate action (correction, expression of concern, retraction, sanctions) when nondisclosure affects the integrity of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full written disclosure as the backbone of COI management
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts of interest cannot be eliminated altogether but can be managed; the backbone of managing conflicts of interest is full written disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require complete, written declarations as the foundation for subsequent editorial assessment and management. Recognize disclosure is an imperfect remedy and that editors must still determine whether disclosed interests impair objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local tailoring of operational definitions and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: WAME does not prescribe a universal standard for when meaningful conflict of interest exists; instead it defines and recommends elements of COI policies and encourages journals to establish their own operational standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow journals latitude to set thresholds and operational definitions matching discipline, culture, and context. Be mindful that overly broad or rigid lists could paralyze peer review; editors must balance comprehensiveness with feasibility when setting local standards.
